title: Working alone, in carparks and near traffic
verdict: I would not sign this and I would not send a technician out on it. The legal skeleton is the best in the set — I checked every section against legislation.qld.gov.au and ss 36, 38, 40, 42, 43, 48, 69, 79(3), 289, 291, 292, 299 (including the genuine s 299(4)), 300, 301, 302, 303, 317(1)(b) of the Regulation and ss 38, 38(7), 39 of the Act all say what the document claims — and the traffic discipline, the confined-space refusal and the communications step are the work of somebody who has actually stood in a basement. It fails on the room it walks the technician into and never looks at. The statement puts a lone technician in a fire pump room "with the pump running" twice (steps[2].hazards[2], steps[7].hazards[5]) and controls the noise and the heat and nothing else: the pumpset is never named as a machine that starts by itself on a falling pressure — which is exactly what steps[7].controls[1] tells the technician to create — the jockey pump and the controller selector appear nowhere, the coupling and fan are never mentioned, and diesel exhaust in a closed basement room is never named at all, while step 2's carbon-monoxide controls are scoped to vehicle exhaust and the carpark fans. The company's own sprinkler statement says put both controllers out of auto before any pressure is allowed to fall, and its own hydrant statement says "Nobody runs a diesel fire pump alone, on any site, for any reason" and sets a minimum of two people for any full-bore flow — yet whenRequired dispatches "hydrant flow tests at the street" as a lone visit and nothing routes a pump run or a charged line out to that statement the way height and confined space are properly routed out. The three hard lines need to be five. Behind that sit a named hazard with no control at all (the lift going to fire mode, steps[11].hazards[2]), no provision anywhere for the pedestrians who have to get past a footpath the statement lets one person close, and a carbon monoxide monitor ranked as an engineering control with no calibration, bump test or alarm set point required of it. Fix those and it is close to the best statement here; as it stands a technician reading it believes the pump room is handled.

blocking.problem: steps[7].controls[0] names the only isolation points as "the booster isolation valve, or the section stop valve in the valve room" and controls[1] then says "Drain or vent to a safe point ... and prove zero on the gauge before a cap or a gland is touched". Nothing in the statement isolates the system's automatic pressure sources. The fire pump and the jockey pump are never named as controllers that have an AUTO selector; the words "jockey pump", "pumpset", "controller" and "auto" do not appear anywhere in the document. A draining or venting operation is a falling-pressure event: through a stop valve that passes, or where the wrong point was chosen, the jockey pump makes the line up again and the fire pump starts, and a line proved at zero one minute is live the next with a cap off it. The same start puts a coupling, shaft and fan into motion in a room a lone technician is standing in, with no start-up warning and nobody to hit stop. The company's own sprinkler-wet statement carries the control this one is missing — "On a pumped system, put the fire pump and the jockey pump controllers OUT OF AUTO at the controller selector, and hang your tag on each, BEFORE any pressure is allowed to fall" — so this is a correction that was made elsewhere and never landed here.
blocking.fix: Insert a new isolate-level control at steps[7].controls[1], pushing the existing drain control to [2]: "On a pumped system, before any pressure is allowed to fall: put the fire pump and the jockey pump controllers OUT OF AUTO at the selector on the outside of the cubicle — never open a controller door — and hang your own danger tag on each. Photograph both selectors. A stop valve that passes plus a jockey pump in auto will put pressure back into a line you proved at zero, and a pumpset in auto starts on the pressure drop your own drain creates, with nobody in the room to stop it. Both go back to AUTO at check-out (Step 14), confirmed by eye against the arrival photograph and recorded on the job." Add an administrative control after the existing controls[3]: "Whenever any pump is in auto, treat the coupling, shaft and fan as live — no hand, tool, rag or torch near them, never stand in line with the coupling, sleeves down and nothing hanging. There is no warning and no start delay." Add to steps[13].controls[1]: "...and that the fire and jockey pump controllers are back in AUTO, confirmed by eye against the arrival photograph."

blocking.problem: The hazard is stated as "Pump room noise while the pump runs" and the only control that answers it is steps[7].controls[7], PPE: "Hearing protection on before the pump starts, at the class recorded for that plant room." The statement therefore accepts, in writing, that a lone technician will be in an enclosed basement plant room with a fire pump running, and treats the pump as a noise source and nothing else. If it is a diesel set, running it in a closed room produces carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide, and the hot manifold and flue are burn hazards — none of which are named anywhere in this document. Step 2, the CO step, is written entirely around vehicle exhaust and the carpark exhaust fans, and steps[2].controls[2] scopes the CO monitor to "any after-hours or closed-up basement visit", so on a daytime visit with a diesel running there is no monitor requirement at all. The document's own steps[2].hazards[3] says the point plainly — "CO and heat both take your judgement before they take your consciousness, so a lone worker will not self-rescue" — and then never applies it to the one engine on the site. The company's hydrant-flow statement is unambiguous: "Nobody runs a diesel fire pump alone, on any site, for any reason", with a standby person outside the door, a verified flue and mechanical ventilation running. This statement's screening list at steps[0].controls[1] has four exclusions and a pump run is not one of them.
blocking.fix: Insert a new eliminate-level control at steps[7].controls[0], ahead of the isolation control: "NO PUMP RUN ON A LONE VISIT. A lone technician does not start, does not cause to start, and does not remain in a room with a running fire pump — electric or diesel. Nobody runs a diesel fire pump alone, on any site, for any reason: the exhaust is carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide in a closed room, the noise is past the exposure standard, the manifold and flue will burn you, and there is nobody outside the door. Pump runs are booked as a crewed visit under the Hydrant and Booster Flow Testing and Pump Testing SWMS, which sets a minimum of two people for any pump run and a standby person outside the room for the whole run. If a pump starts while you are in the room, leave the room." Add it as a fourth hard line in whenRequired and as a fifth item in the steps[0].controls[1] screening list ("no pump run, and no work in a room with a pump running"). Amend steps[2].controls[2] and the matching ppe entry to read "...for any visit below ground, and any time you are in a room with an engine running."

blocking.problem: whenRequired lists the lone-visit workload as "Booster services, hydrant flow tests at the street, carpark detectors and heads, basement plant rooms, and after-hours call-outs", and steps[7] duly covers the flow gauge (controls[5]) and "A hydrant discharge running across a footpath, a shared path or a traffic lane" (hazards[2]). The company's own statement for that work sets a different rule: "Minimum two people for any full-bore flow, any booster test and any pump run" and "One person on the landing valve, one at the diffuser, in sight of each other or on the radio, with an agreed hand signal for STOP that either can give. Nobody works alone on a charged line." So this statement dispatches one person to work the company's own two-person job. The hazards that make it a two-person job are not named here at all: reaction on a charged 65 mm line and standpipe, a hose that gets away with nobody at the landing valve to shut it, and taking a pitot reading at the jet. The routing that exists for height ("goes to a crewed visit under the working-at-height SWMS") and for confined spaces ("rebook it as a crewed visit under the confined space SWMS") is simply absent for flow testing, and there is no cross-reference anywhere in the document to the flow-testing statement.
blocking.fix: Strike "hydrant flow tests at the street" from the lone-visit list in whenRequired, and add a fourth hard line: "4. Charged lines and flow tests. A lone technician may inspect, read gauges, check caps and glands on a drained and proved line, and do the paperwork. A full-bore hydrant flow, a booster flow test and any work on a charged line are not lone work — there is nobody on the landing valve to shut it and nobody to give the STOP signal. They are booked as a crewed shift under the Hydrant and Booster Flow Testing and Pump Testing SWMS, minimum two people." Add the matching eliminate-level control as steps[7].controls[1] (after the no-pump-run control): "No full-bore flow, no booster flow test and no work on a charged line alone. If the job as scoped needs one, stop, ring the supervisor and have it rebooked crewed — the charged line, the standpipe reaction and the pitot reading all assume a second person, and this statement does not give you one." Add the same item to the steps[0].controls[1] screening list and a site prompt: "Does today's scope include a full-bore flow or a booster test? If it does, today is not a lone visit."

blocking.problem: The step names "The lift going to fire mode with the technician on B3" as a hazard and then never controls it. All eight controls in steps[11] are about calling for help, being struck on the frontage, the missed check-in, water, CO, the first aid kit and notification. The only place the lift appears again is inside the 000 script at steps[11].controls[1] — "whether the lift is usable" — which asks the technician to report the problem, not to prevent or fix it. Nothing tells the technician that their own detector or panel test is what sends every lift in the building to fire mode; nothing tells them not to plan a heavy carry out on a lift they are about to disable; nothing has anybody restore lift service; and the ambulance's stretcher route out of B3 is left to be discovered at the worst moment. The emergency prose covers a fire alarm evacuation ("leave by the fire stair, not the vehicle ramp") but that is a different event and it is not a control in the step.
blocking.fix: Insert an administrative control at steps[11].controls[1], after the get-to-a-signal control: "LIFTS AND YOUR OWN TESTING. Any alarm you generate below ground sends the lifts to fire mode — your way out, and the ambulance's way in, becomes the fire stair. Before any test that can recall the lifts, tell the building manager or concierge it is coming and confirm who can restore lift service and how fast. Take nothing below ground you cannot carry back up a stair on your own. On 000, say whether the lifts are in fire mode and whether anyone on site can release them." Add to steps[13].controls[1]: "...and confirm the lifts are out of fire mode and back in normal service, and note who restored them." Add a site prompt: "Who can put this building's lifts back into normal service after a test, and how are they contacted after hours?"

blocking.problem: The statement lets one person work "on a footpath that is properly closed" (whenRequired, hard line 1; repeated at steps[12].controls[0], "devices behind the kerb line or on a closed footpath"), and steps[5].hazards[3] names "Bags, drums and hose across a public footpath". No control anywhere says how a pedestrian gets past. steps[5].controls[2] warns the path approach with "a device on the FOOTPATH approach as well as the road approach" and steps[7].controls[5] keeps the gear tidy, but a warning device is not a route. "Properly closed" is never defined, and the statement never says who may close a footpath or where the people on it are supposed to go — so the foreseeable outcome is a pedestrian, a pram, a wheelchair or a person using a cane stepping around a coned booster and into the trafficked lane the whole of Step 6 exists to keep the technician out of. A cane user gets no warning from a cone at knee height and no warning at all from a hose lying across the path. This is the one traffic exposure the statement creates for other people rather than for the technician, and it is the only one it does not manage.
blocking.fix: Insert an isolate-level control at steps[5].controls[2], ahead of the existing zone control: "PEDESTRIANS GET A ROUTE OR THE PATH DOES NOT GET CLOSED. Keep a continuous unobstructed path past the work on the same side, at least 1.2 m wide, level, with no hose across it — a hose crossing goes under a ramp or it does not cross. Barriers on the path side are continuous and detectable at ground level by a cane, not single cones with gaps between them. If that width cannot be kept behind the kerb, the footpath closure and the pedestrian detour come from the approved Traffic Guidance Scheme and are set by a crew: a lone technician never closes a footpath, and never sends pedestrians onto the road, into a lane, or across to the other side." Amend hard line 1 in whenRequired to read "...or on a footpath where a compliant pedestrian route past the work is kept open; closing a footpath and detouring pedestrians is crewed work under an approved scheme." Add a site prompt: "Can a 1.2 m pedestrian path be kept past the booster? If not, today is a crewed visit."

blocking.problem: The personal CO monitor is listed at level "engineering". It is not an engineering control — it changes nothing about the atmosphere, it only warns — and putting it at that level ranks a detection device above every administrative control in the step and reads as though the air has been made safe. Worse than the label is what the control omits. The step itself says a lone worker will not self-rescue from CO, which makes this monitor the last thing standing between the technician and the floor, and the specification for it is "switched on and clipped at chest height" — no calibration currency, no bump test, no alarm set points. A CO sensor out of calibration reads low or reads nothing, and steps[11].controls[5] hangs the whole leave-immediately trigger on "CO monitor in alarm". The company's own hydrant-flow statement specifies the monitor properly: "calibration in date, bump tested this morning, low and high alarms set below the carbon monoxide exposure limit". The scope is also wrong — "any after-hours or closed-up basement visit" leaves a daytime plant room with an engine running uncovered.
blocking.fix: Re-level this control to "ppe" and move it to the end of the steps[2] control list, after the administrative controls, so the hierarchy reads correctly, and rewrite it as: "Personal CO monitor, calibration in date and bump tested that morning, low and high alarms set below the carbon monoxide exposure standard, switched on and clipped at chest height for any visit below ground and any time you are in a room with an engine running. In alarm you leave immediately by the nearest stair, not after you finish the device you are on. A monitor that is out of calibration, out of bump test, or sitting in the ute is not a monitor: without one you do not go below ground, you ring the supervisor and it is rebooked." Amend the matching ppe entry to the same wording. For consistency, apply the same re-levelling to steps[4].controls[0]: the duress device is already listed in the ppe array and is a notification device, not an engineering control.

blocking.problem: steps[1].controls[0], at eliminate level, tells the technician to "Park in the visitor bay or the loading zone at ground level and walk the gear in ... taking the ute down the ramp buys ten metres and a headroom problem", and steps[1].controls[4] reinforces it ("park up top and carry"). Two later controls then depend on the vehicle being in the basement: steps[8].controls[2] "put the work vehicle between the ladder and the approach where the aisle is long", and steps[10].controls[0]-[1], which use "the work vehicle or a barrier between you and the approach" and then say of the beacon, "In a dim carpark it is the only thing that reads as 'work in progress' rather than 'someone getting into their car'." A technician who follows the preferred control in Step 2 arrives at the ladder and the aisle with no shadow vehicle and no beacon, and the control the document calls the only thing that reads as a work zone silently does not exist. Nothing in the statement notices the conflict or supplies a substitute.
blocking.fix: Amend steps[1].controls[0] to end: "— and because the ute stays up top, the beacon and the shadow vehicle go with it, so the battery amber beacon and a lit A-frame barrier come in with the gear." Add them to the ppe/equipment list. Amend steps[10].controls[1] to: "Amber beacon running — on the parked vehicle where it is with you, otherwise the battery beacon stood upstream of the work at the edge of the coned area. In a dim carpark it is the only thing that reads as 'work in progress' rather than 'someone getting into their car', so one of the two is always running: a coned bay with no light is not a work zone down here." Amend steps[8].controls[2] to: "...and put the work vehicle, or a lit A-frame barrier where the vehicle is at ground level, between the ladder and the approach where the aisle is long."
